name: Eye support

card.summary: Eye support is the looksmaxxing term for how well the orbital rim, cheekbones and surrounding tissue hold the eyes and lower lids in place, and improving it (through fillers, fat grafting or implants) is meant to give a firmer, more open and rested eye area.
card.aka: under-eye support; orbital support; orbital vector
card.note: Procedures that change the orbital area carry eye-specific surgical risks and are done by specialist surgeons.

quick.overview:
Eye support is a community term for how firmly the bone and soft tissue under and around the eye hold the lower lid and eyeball in position. Forum members treat it as a core part of the eye area: strong support is described as giving a lifted lower lid, little white showing below the iris and a rested look, while weak support is linked to hollowness, dark shadows and a tired or bulging appearance.

The concept overlaps with real anatomy. Surgical papers describe the lower eyelid as held by a fibrous orbital support system, muscle tone and fat compartments, and describe aging as a weakening of those supports. Looksmaxxers discuss the orbital vector (how far the eyeball sits in front of the cheek's rim) as a shorthand for the bone side of this.
quick.how: Discussion centres on what can be changed: filler or fat grafting under the eye to add volume, infraorbital rim or cheek implants and other facial-bone surgery from a surgeon, lower-lid procedures such as blepharoplasty, and general leanness or body-fat changes that alter facial fullness. Some members also ask about collagen supplements or under-eye exercises, which are usually answered with the point that the underlying issue is skeletal.
quick.risks: Any treatment near the eye can affect the lids and vision; surgical literature on the orbit describes complications such as swelling, bruising, infection and lid position changes, and filler in this area is typically placed by experienced clinicians. Forum suggestions such as bone smashing near the orbit are met with warnings from other members about eye injury.

lead: Eye support is a looksmaxxing term for how well the orbital rim, the cheekbone region and the soft tissue under the eye hold the eye and lower lid in place. In community rating frameworks it sits among the main eye-area factors alongside canthal tilt and eyelid exposure. Members use it to describe a firm, lifted lower lid with the eyes sitting comfortably set against the cheek, versus a hollow or sagging under-eye with extra white showing.

The concept borrows from clinical anatomy. A 2024 plastic-surgery paper on lower-eyelid blepharoplasty describes aging of the lower lid in terms of a weakened fibrous orbital support system, reduced muscle tone and increased orbital fat, and tailors surgery to those findings [1]. Surgeons also discuss orbital support in reconstruction, where restoring the orbital floor or midface bone restores lid and eye position [2].

On looksmax.org the topic appears in threads on the orbital vector, fillers and implants for under-eye support, fat grafting, and whether weight or buccal fat changes alter it [3][4][5]. Members debate how much is determined by bone versus fat pads, and whether infraorbital rim implants really change lower-lid support.

Clinical literature supplies the anatomy behind the term. A 2025 review of infraorbital hollows describes aging of the under-eye region as involving bone resorption, weakening of the orbicularis muscle, fat atrophy and herniation, and thinning skin, and recommends addressing midface volume before treating the hollow directly [15]. Lower-lid surgery uses canthal support procedures and fat repositioning along the orbital rim to maintain lid position and smooth the lid-cheek transition [14].

chain: Under-eye volume and orbital rim projection are increased (fillers, fat, implants)
Lower lid is held higher and less hollow
Eyes look more open, rested and youthful
angle.text: People who want a firmer eye area use eye support as the target for treatments aimed at adding structure beneath the lid, such as filler, fat grafting and midface or rim implants. The stated goal is a lifted lower lid, less shadowing and a more rested look.

paras: In looksmaxxing usage, eye support refers to the structural backing of the eye: the bone of the infraorbital rim and maxilla, the cheek fat, and the lid tissues that hold the lower lid against the globe. Threads describe good support as a lid margin that sits at or slightly above the lower edge of the iris with a smooth lid-cheek transition, and poor support as scleral show, hollowing or a tear-trough groove [3][6].

A related idea is the orbital vector, a line comparing the front of the eyeball with the cheek's infraorbital rim. A user in one thread argues the vector is determined largely by under-eye fat and tissue rather than bone forward growth alone, and replies recommend fat grafting or implants depending on the case [3].

A 2024 study of 137 patients aged 20 to 60 classified lower-eyelid aging into three morphologies and linked them to a weakened fibrous orbital support system, reduced muscle tone and increased orbital fat [1]. A general review of the ocular adnexa outlines the eyelid, lacrimal and ocular-surface structures involved [7].

In facial reconstruction literature, restoring orbital floor or midface bone is described as restoring orbital support and eye position, for example in delayed orbital floor repair using autologous cartilage and iliac bone grafts in two patients [2].

The orbital vector compares how far the front of the eyeball sits relative to the cheek's infraorbital rim. Looksmaxxers describe a positive, neutral or negative vector, and a negative vector is commonly linked to a recessed look beneath the eye [3]. One widely shared argument on looksmax.org holds that the eyeball sits in front of the rim in virtually everyone, so the vector is mostly a function of under-eye tissue and fat rather than bone alone [3].

Neighbouring terms include scleral show (white visible below the iris), lower eyelid exposure, tear trough (the groove running down from the inner corner of the eye), dark circles and fox eye. Threads on each frequently loop back to support [6][11][13].

The 2025 Aesthetic Surgery Journal Open Forum review defines infraorbital hollows as the tear trough medially and the palpebromalar groove laterally. It describes younger patients with mild to moderate hollows, thicker skin and little laxity as the best candidates, and deep grooves, pronounced bags, thin skin or significant laxity as less favourable [15].

Its authors recommend addressing midface volume loss first, with direct treatment close to the orbital rim as a second step, and describe a consensus of conservative correction with optional touch-ups. They list oedema, surface irregularity, the Tyndall effect, filler migration and vascular danger zones among the complications, and disclose consulting relationships with a filler manufacturer [15].
Hyaluronic acid fillers can be reversed with hyaluronidase if the outcome is unwanted, as covered in the wiki's article on filler dissolving.

Lower-lid blepharoplasty approaches the eyelid from the skin side or from inside the lid. Adjunct techniques include canthopexy or canthoplasty to stabilise the outer corner and keep the lid in position, fat repositioning along the infraorbital rim to smooth the eyelid-cheek transition and tear trough, and autologous fat transfer to restore periorbital volume [14]. A Wikipedia entry on the procedure traces the term to 1818, when Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coined it for eyelid reconstruction after cancer surgery [14].
The 2024 Annals of Plastic Surgery series tailored surgery to three lower-lid morphologies in 137 patients aged 20 to 60, treating support weakness, muscle tone and fat as separate contributors [1].

Looksmaxxers also discuss infraorbital rim and malar implants and other facial-bone procedures. Forum posters disagree about whether rim implants themselves deliver lid support, with one thread arguing they do not and another recommending implants over fat grafting where scleral show is present at rest [10][3]. In reconstructive literature, restoring orbital floor or midface bone is described as restoring orbital support and eye position after trauma or tumour surgery [2].

Forum threads cover a range: filler to add volume under the eye, fat grafting, infraorbital rim implants, surgeries for scleral show, buccal fat questions and whether gaining weight helped [8][9]. One thread title holds that rim implants do not by themselves provide under-eye support, illustrating disagreement over which procedure addresses which problem [10].

Other threads ask about collagen supplements and under-eye exercises. Replies to a collagen question note that supplementing is low-cost but that the issue is mostly skeletal [11]. A thread proposing bone smashing for canthal tilt drew replies calling it ineffective and warning of eye injury [12].

Other threads ask about gaining body fat, buccal fat and under-eye exercises as ways to alter the area [8][16][17]. A thread titled around what can be done for poor lower-eye support gathers many of these ideas in one place [5].

No studies found that test 'eye support' as a defined measure. Related surgical literature describes lower-eyelid anatomy and treatment: a 2024 series of 137 blepharoplasty patients with 1 to 12 months of follow-up tailored surgery to each lower-lid morphology [1], and case reports describe orbital floor reconstruction restoring orbital support after trauma [2].

Eye support appears in rating threads next to canthal tilt, eye-area ratio and brow ridge as one of the checks members apply to photographs, and members tag threads with 'gtfih' (go the f*** in hardmode) calls for detailed advice [4][7]. Its use is mostly diagnostic: people post photos and ask whether support is positive or negative, then discuss fillers, implants or surgery [3][5][13].

timeline.event: Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coins the term blepharoplasty for eyelid reconstruction, per Wikipedia [14].
A review of ocular surface and adnexal anatomy summarises lid and orbit structures [7].
A 137-patient lower-eyelid blepharoplasty series links lid aging to orbital support, muscle tone and fat [1].
An infraorbital hollow review recommends midface support before direct treatment [15].

lore.intro: Eye support is a staple term in looksmax.org eye-area discussions, usually paired with orbital vector and scleral show [3][6].

claims.claim: Under-eye support is mostly determined by bone, so little can change it without surgery
claims.believers: Members say the issue is skeletal and that collagen or similar supplements are unlikely to change it, while implants or grafting might [11][3].
claims.experts: Surgical papers describe lower-lid appearance as depending on fibrous support, muscle tone and fat as well as the underlying bone [1].

claims.claim: Fillers or fat grafting can improve under-eye support
claims.believers: Some members recommend fillers or fat grafting for negative vectors, with implants preferred where scleral show is present [3][13].
claims.experts: Published literature on lower-lid treatment centres on blepharoplasty techniques tailored to fat and support findings [1]; no trials define a measure called eye support.

claims.claim: Bone smashing near the orbit can improve eye support or canthal tilt
claims.believers: The poster proposing it argues swelling could change the eye area [12].
claims.experts: No published studies support it, and other forum members respond that it risks eye injury [12].

claims.claim: Gaining body fat improves under-eye support
claims.believers: A thread asks who improved support by gaining weight, reflecting a belief that under-eye and cheek fat influences the vector [8][3].
claims.experts: Surgical papers describe orbital fat as contributing both to bags when herniated and to fullness, depending on distribution [1][15].

claims.believers: One thread asks about exercises to gain support back [17].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined exercises for under-eye support; clinical reviews describe bone, ligament, fat and muscle changes as the basis of aging in the area [15].

claims.claim: Midface volume should be treated before the under-eye hollow
claims.believers: Forum threads on fillers discuss targeting the vector and the cheek together [4].
claims.experts: The 2025 review recommends addressing midface volume loss before direct infraorbital treatment [15].
